reading.body:
Suno and Udio trained their music generation systems on copyrighted music scraped from the internet without permission. Record labels demonstrated that the systems could recreate recognizable versions of copyrighted songs when prompted with descriptions matching the originals. The systems were deployed to generate music for users while their training data sources remained undisclosed.

This is a model trained on data obtained without rights clearance, then deployed commercially. It could have been caught by obtaining licenses before training, by documenting training sources from the outset, or by declining to recreate identifiable copyrighted works. A German court ruled against Suno in a copyright case brought by GEMA. It is not established what proportion of training data was infringing, or whether the systems' output necessarily infringes when it resembles copyrighted works.

summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, and Warner Music have sued AI music generators Udio and Suno, claiming they scraped thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their systems. The labels filed separate lawsuits in New York and Massachusetts, alleging that both companies deliberately copied massive amounts of music and can now recreate versions of famous songs by famous artists. The record companies claim the companies refuse to disclose which songs they used for training and have falsely defended the practice as fair use.

To support their case, the record labels demonstrated they could generate AI songs that closely replicate famous tracks by using specific prompts describing the original songs' characteristics, decade, genre, and artist style. They recreated versions resembling songs by artists including The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Chuck Berry, and Mariah Carey. The labels submitted thousands of specific copyrighted works they claim were scraped, along with a thumb drive of AI-generated music examples showing the similarities. The lawsuit represents a major legal battle about how generative AI services can use existing creative work to train their models.
